conversation.assistant:
You’re right to be a bit cautious here—HVAC is one of those areas where it’s easy to get oversold if you don’t have a baseline to work from.

The good news is, for routine maintenance, you can keep this very controlled. You’re not asking them to diagnose a failing system—you’re just asking for a standard service. That alone cuts down a lot of the nonsense.

When you call, frame it simply:
“I’m looking to have routine maintenance done on my HVAC system—just a standard check and service. What’s included, and what do you charge for that?”

A solid company will give you a clear, almost boring answer. Typically, a maintenance visit should include:
- Inspecting and cleaning components (coils, blower, etc.)
- Checking refrigerant levels (for AC/heat pump)
- Testing system operation
- Looking at electrical connections
- Replacing or checking filters (sometimes you provide the filter)

If they immediately start steering the conversation toward upgrades, memberships, or “we’ll see what you need when we get there,” that’s a mild yellow flag—not a dealbreaker, but something to note.

A few practical things to watch for:

First, pricing clarity  
You want to hear something like “Our maintenance visit is $X” or a clear range. Vague answers tend to lead to surprises.

Second, how they talk about problems  
A trustworthy tech will explain findings in plain terms and give you options.  
Be cautious if you hear:
- “This really needs to be replaced soon” without a clear reason
- Pressure to decide on the spot
- Big-ticket recommendations based on age alone

Age matters, but it’s not a diagnosis.

Third, documentation  
After the visit, you should get a summary—what they checked, what they found, anything to keep an eye on. That alone filters out a lot of less professional outfits.

If they do suggest something expensive, a very simple line protects you:
“Alright, I’d like to think that over. Can you write that up for me?”

A legitimate issue will still be there tomorrow. Pressure is usually the giveaway.

One more small advantage you have: even if HVAC isn’t your specialty, you understand systems, maintenance cycles, and how things fail. You’ll pick up quickly whether someone is explaining a real issue or just talking around one.

If I were in your position, I’d approach this the same way as the plumber:
Pick a well-reviewed local company, book a basic service, and treat it as a first meeting. You’re not committing to them long-term—you’re seeing how they operate.

And if you want, after you make a few calls, you can come back and run their answers by me. I can help you sanity-check what they’re telling you before you book anything.
